Reb Yisrael Yosef expected that it would take Yoel some time to get over the shock of the whole story, and to get used to the idea of going to Reb Eliyahu Baal Shem’s yeshiva. Neither Yoel nor his peers had ever learned kabbalah before.

But Yoel was actually excited. For Yoel’s teacher, Rav Yoel Sirkis, was

better known as “the Bach”—an acronym for his sefer called Bayis Chadash, a great work of halacha.

But in addition to his halachic knowledge, the Bach was also a master of kabbalah. Over the young Yoel’s five years of learning in Brisk, he found out that his teacher had a secret kabbalah class. Yoel was interested, and tried to attend. But he wasn’t allowed; only a select few older married students were permitted to join. Now that he’d be going to Prague, Yoel could pursue learning kabbalah, and with his father’s blessing!

When Yoel came to the yeshiva in Prague, Reb Eliyahu Baal Shem was already quite old and didn’t teach as much anymore. It was his students who ran the yeshiva, while he mostly spent his days locked away in his room, learning by himself. But with Yoel’s arrival, things were different. The Baal Shem took a liking to him, and spent many hours personally teaching him both the secrets of kabbalah and his healing remedies.

Despite being one of the youngest and newest students of Reb Eliyahu Baal Shem, Yoel soon became the greatest. The Baal Shem taught him the most, and praised him highly. After spending five years in Prague, Reb Eliyahu instructed Yoel to return to Zamostch. Soon after, the entire area buzzed with excitement: There was now a new Baal Shem—Reb Yoel of Zamostch.

Meanwhile, back in Prague, Shmuel—now known as Reb Shmuel, the devoted Rosh Hakahal—was sitting at his large desk in the rauthaus. The room was empty of all others; as usual, he was still working in his office long after the day’s meetings were over.

Reb Shmuel leaned over a wooden ledger in front of him. “3,000 … 5,000 … 2,000 …” He

held a candle in his right hand, and ran his left finger down the lines which marked the collected payments. When he was done, he shook his head. That year had been a hard one for the community of Prague; the va’ad had only been able to collect half of the required Jewish communal taxes. They still needed another few thousand thalers. Once again, Reb Shmuel would have to pay for the difference himself.

There was a knock at the door. “Reb Shmuel,” the visitor, head of

the community chevra kadisha, doffed his hat and bowed his head. “We’ve reviewed your request. We

are sorry, but it seems that it just isn’t possible.”

Reb Shmuel straightened. “What, exactly, is not possible?”

plot designated for you! It is right at the center of the cemetery,

right next to the previous Rosh Hakahal, Reb Mordechai Meisel! And just a few rows away from your zeide’s kever. It’s beaut—”

Reb Shmuel silenced him by lifting up an index finger. “Let me show you something.” Reb Shmuel thrust his hand into his drawer, and pulled out a yellowing parchment, still tied with the same brown string from some fifty years before. He fumbled with the string and spread it out on the table. “Here,” he pointed at the critical line written in his grandfather’s signature script.

He lowered his glasses to the top of his nose, mouthed the words as he read and nodded. Though the once-black ink was now a faded gray and the parchment was crumbling at the edges, you could still make out the words: “Rav Betzalel ben Harav Yehuda

to the owner of this deed,” Reb Shmuel said. “The first was given to my zeide, zecher tzaddik livracha, some fifty years ago. The second to my bubbe, zichrona livracha. The third remains unoccupied, and rightfully belongs to the name listed.”

one hundred percent correct, Reb Shmuel. I understand that having this plot is your wish.”

certainly. Your grandfather was the giant of the generation, masterful speaker,

inspirer of hearts, healer of souls, and his sefarim! Oy, his sefarim, I learn them every Shabbos.”

no room in the cemetery, Reb Shmuel. So many people wanted the privilege of being buried next to your illustrious zeide. The chevra kadisha have done the best they could. They squeezed in another kever here, another there, and now—” He held up his two index fingers in front of his face, an inch apart from each other. “This is all the space that is left.”

Reb Shmuel let out a sigh that turned into a cough. After a drink of water, he straightened his shoulders and looked at the visitor once more. “I understand that you are in a predicament. However, I stand by my right to the kever. Here is my advice: Please gather a minyan to daven at my zeide’s grave, and remind him of his promise. I’m sure he will deliver.”

Source: Yiddish Memoirs Vol. I, pp. 327-328 / English Memoirs Vol. II, pp. 88-89.
